<awtsmoosMeluketTranslation heichel="ikar" alias="meluket_translation_en" seriesId="חשון_meluket" postId="BH_POST_1766518914964_theRebbe_974" batchId="meluket-_D7_97_D7_A9_D7_95_D7_9F_meluket__BH_POST_1766518914964_theRebbe_974__p002">
  <section v="3">
    <sectionSummaryBrief>Through repentance out of love, the past is transformed, enabling all one's years to be equal for good, and this explains the connection between the two interpretations of Sarah's life.</sectionSummaryBrief>
    <t s="0">And one can explain the elucidation of this,</t>
    <t s="1">that through repentance out of love, even the past is changed,</t>
    <t s="2">and therefore it is within the power of each person</t>
    <t s="3">(even one who sinned and blemished and transgressed the path)</t>
    <t s="4">that all his years</t>
    <t s="5">(even his years of the past)</t>
    <t s="6">should be equal for good.</t>
    <t s="7">And based on this, one can explain the connection and relevance of the two interpretations of “the years of the life of Sarah,”</t>
    <t s="8">that “all of them were equally good,”</t>
    <t s="9">for all matters in physicality descend from their counterpart in spirituality,</t>
    <t s="10">and through the matter of “all of them were life” regarding supernal life,</t>
    <t s="11">thereby it is brought about that “all of them were life” also regarding life in its simple sense,</t>
    <t s="12">that the life is hers and she becomes the master over them,</t>
    <t s="13">and through this, power is given to every Jew</t>
    <t s="14">that all the years of his life</t>
    <t s="15">(even the years that have passed)</t>
    <t s="16">should be his and that he should be the master over them,</t>
    <t s="17">and therefore it is in his power that all his years</t>
    <t s="18">(even the years of the past)</t>
    <t s="19">should be equal for good.</t>
  </section>
  <section v="4">
    <sectionSummaryBrief>Every Jew can be a Beinoni at any time through free will to fulfill the mitzvah of repentance, which reveals the innate repentance within, making past transgressions as if they never occurred.</sectionSummaryBrief>
    <t s="0">3)</t>
    <t s="1">And based on this, one can understand what is written in Tanya,</t>
    <t s="2">that every person can be a Beinoni at any time and any hour,</t>
    <t s="3">for at first glance,</t>
    <t s="4">since a Beinoni is one who never committed a transgression in his life and was never called wicked even for one hour or one moment all his days,</t>
    <t s="5">how can every person</t>
    <t s="6">(including even one who committed a transgression)</t>
    <t s="7">be a Beinoni?</t>
    <t s="8">And one can explain the elucidation of this,</t>
    <t s="9">that just as regarding all the mitzvos, permission is given to every person and there is none who can prevent him,</t>
    <t s="10">so too is it regarding the mitzvah of repentance,</t>
    <t s="11">that every Jew has free choice to fulfill the mitzvah of repentance.</t>
    <t s="12">And one can say,</t>
    <t s="13">that the choice regarding the mitzvah of repentance is even greater than regarding other mitzvos.</t>
    <t s="14">Because repentance is a general mitzvah,</t>
    <t s="15">and therefore there is a special empowerment given for it.</t>
    <t s="16">And also,</t>
    <t s="17">since every Jew wants to fulfill all the mitzvos and distance himself from transgressions, only his evil inclination overpowered him,</t>
    <t s="18">so when he committed a transgression, contrary to the will of his true self,</t>
    <t s="19">in his innermost being he regrets and is distressed and worried about it.</t>
    <t s="20">That is,</t>
    <t s="21">that in his innermost being he repents</t>
    <t s="22">immediately.</t>
    <t s="23">And therefore, that there is none who can prevent him from fulfilling the mitzvah of repentance is</t>
    <t s="24">(in a particular sense)</t>
    <t s="25">greater than regarding other mitzvos,</t>
    <t s="26">for in order to fulfill this mitzvah, he does not need a new action or deed, only to reveal the repentance that is in his innermost being.</t>
    <t s="27">And this is that every person can be a Beinoni at any time and any hour,</t>
    <t s="28">for since he has free choice to fulfill the mitzvah of repentance,</t>
    <t s="29">and the essence and perfection of repentance is repentance out of love,</t>
    <t s="30">through which his transgression is uprooted from its very beginning,</t>
    <t s="31">so it is within his ability to be a Beinoni who never committed a transgression in his life.</t>
  </section>
  <section v="5">
    <sectionSummaryBrief>Each interpretation of Sarah's life includes the other, as the concept of all being equal for good contains the idea of life being hers, and vice versa.</sectionSummaryBrief>
    <t s="0">4)</t>
    <t s="1">And one may add in explaining the connection and relevance of the two interpretations of “the years of the life of Sarah,”</t>
    <t s="2">that “all of them were life” and “all of them were equal,”</t>
    <t s="3">that in each of them both matters are included.</t>
    <t s="4">For also in the interpretation that “the years of the life of Sarah” means they were all equally good,</t>
    <t s="5">the matter of “all of them were life” is included</t>
    <t s="6">[as above in section 2,</t>
    <t s="7">that in order for all to be equally good, even the years of the past,</t>
    <t s="8">it is through that the years of his life are his],</t>
    <t s="9">and likewise conversely,</t>
    <t s="10">that also in the interpretation that “the years of the life of Sarah” means “all of them were life,”</t>
    <t s="11">the matter of “all of them were equal” is included.</t>
  </section>
</awtsmoosMeluketTranslation>
